chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Jazz as advanced music and the mass audience
summary: Wilson says jazz is more technically advanced than rock, likens audience levels to classical music, and sees the swing era as the best meeting of musicians and the public.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: But see, jazz though, is a highly technically advanced way of music; it's much more advanced technically than rock and roll.
Just like the classical music, the music that the symphony plays is far different from the folk music of the man in the street.
The classical audience is just a small part of that great big audience that makes gold records. The Boston Symphony don't make gold records, or the New York Philharmonic.
But still, you can't say that the majority is the only criteria, because the mass of people don't go to Carnegie Hall and make Carnegie Hall no good;
it shows that the masses are that far behind. But at what level they're at, which is maybe the Beatles or that kind of stuff, or folk, or whatever the people who are not musicians like.

Just like, we go into another unfamiliar area of -- if we're not familiar with it as musicians, there may be certain paintings we don't like that the person who lives in the art galleries, the real painting fan -- well, we go occasionally, we might not like the same things that a person -- we might like paintings that a person goes every day to see a painting in the gallery, he gets tired of what we find to be very nice, and he needs something new, something different, to stimulate his interest.

So there's always a dual thing that the music, the classical music on one level, and that level is sort of parallel to the jazz level, too, and then that big pop thing. But the nearest thing to jazz would be the big band area, started I think by Duke and Fletcher Henderson and brought to a tremendous peak by Goodman and Artie Shaw and the Dorseys and Jimmy Lunceford, That period was the nearest to blending a mass audience with good music. The music of the musicians and the public coming together, don't you think?
